newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialist leader warns of fresh unrest.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialist leader warns of fresh unrest.

text.p: The leader of Bulgaria's former ruling Socialists said on Thursday his election opponents were making unrealistic promises and the Balkan country could face fresh unrest if the electorate felt it had been misled.
"If we don't succeed in reducing the social cost of reform, there is a danger of social unrest like we saw in Albania," party leader Georgi Parvanov told Reuters.

The Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) led 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship which toppled the Socialists in February, and is expected to win a parliamentary majority in April 19 elections.

One of the first tasks of the new government will be to implement a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime agreed with the International Monetary Fund. Its targets include bringing down the budget deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP this year from last year's 12 percent.
Closures of loss-making state enterprises will add further to unemployment, which was 13.7 percent in February.

The European Commission announced on Wednesday it would propose a balance of payments aid package of up to 250 million Ecus ($285 million) to help fill the gap left by the IMF standby loan, but at least part of the international assistance must go straight back to lenders in the form of payments on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
"I was surprised to hear our opponents promising everything to everyone when our agreement with the IMF makes such promises impossible," Parvanov said.
"We are much more realistic in our promises as we have already had our problems running the country and have drawn the necessary conclusions."

Opinion polls put support for the UDF at around 60 percent, compared to about 24 percent for the Socialists, who won parliamentary elections in December 1994 but lost support as the economy deteriorated. Parvanov took over as party leader after prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December.
After 30 days of mass protests, the Socialists agreed to give up attempts to form a new cabinet, and President Petar Stoyanov appointed a caretaker cabinet led by Sofia's UDF mayor, Stefan Sofianski.
Sofianski makes frequent media appearances to explain the reforms, but the consensus negotiated by Stoyanov is showing signs of strain as the elections approach.

In a letter to Stoyanov published by Bulgarian newspapers on Monday, Parvanov complained of a lack of transparency by the interim cabinet over the IMF accord and of politically motivated sackings of senior state employees.

His critics dismissed the letter as a political ploy which was not sanctioned by the rest of the party leadership. Party leaders met Stoyanov to discuss their concerns and reaffirmed their commitment to the reform programme.
Sofianski will stand down after the elections and is expected to be replaced by UDF leader Ivan Kostov, whose approval rating in opinion polls is considerably lower.
"If there is no political consensus, it will cause serious problems for the reforms," Parvanov said.
Albania plunged into turmoil when get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed earlier this year and armed rebels took control of the south in a wave of looting and banditry.
The unrest, and the threat of a mass refugee exodus to wealthier, more peaceful countries, focused international attention on the Balkans and the desirability of maintaining stability in the region.
